title: Interview with a Marathon Runner
description: Four recordings about a marathon runner: a radio interview, a talk with his coach, a school talk and a podcast discussion.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Radio interview
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Lan, interviewing a marathon runner called Daniel.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: Welcome to Weekend Talk. My guest today is Daniel, who finished his twentieth marathon last month. Daniel, most people would say that's a bit crazy.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: They do, and they're probably right, Lan. But I started running at thirty-five, mainly because my doctor told me to lose weight. I could hardly run to the end of my road.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: So how did you get from the end of the road to forty-two kilometres?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Very slowly. In the first year I ran three times a week and never more than five kilometres. I made the mistake most beginners make, which was trying to go too far, too fast. Then I got injured and had to stop for two months.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: Did you think about giving up?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Honestly, yes. But a neighbour persuaded me to join a running club. Having people waiting for me on Saturday mornings made it much harder to stay in bed.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: What does a normal week look like now?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Five runs, one long run of about thirty kilometres on Sundays, and two rest days when I do absolutely nothing. People forget that rest is part of the training.

script.speaker: Lan
script.text: And what do you eat before a race?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Pasta, of course, like everyone. Though the night before, I keep it simple. I once tried a spicy curry and I regretted it by kilometre ten.

parts.title: Part 2 · At the training centre
parts.intro: You will hear Daniel talking to his coach, Ruth, about an injury.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Daniel, come in. How's the knee?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Better than last week, but it still hurts when I go downstairs. I'm worried about the race in March.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Which is eight weeks away. That's enough time, provided you're sensible. Have you been running on it?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Only a little. Twice, actually, about five kilometres each time. Well, the second time was more like eight.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Daniel, that's exactly what I told you not to do.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I know, I know. But I felt fine, and I was frightened of losing fitness.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: You won't lose it in a fortnight. What you could lose is the whole season if the injury gets worse. I want you swimming and cycling for two weeks. No running at all.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Swimming? I hate swimming. I sink.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Then you'll have a good reason to improve. Seriously, the water takes the weight off your joints. And I'll give you some strength exercises for your legs. Do them every morning, ten minutes only.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: All right. And if the knee is better after two weeks?

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Then we start again with short, slow runs. If it isn't, I'll send you for a scan.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Understood. Thanks, Ruth. I'll behave, I promise.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: I'll believe it when I see it.

parts.title: Part 3 · A talk to students
parts.intro: You will hear Daniel giving a talk to a group of school students.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Hello, everyone, and thanks for inviting me. I was asked to talk about running, but I'd rather talk about what happens in your head, because that's where marathons are really won or lost.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Around kilometre thirty, almost everybody hits what runners call the wall. Your legs are heavy, your mind is shouting at you to stop, and the finish line feels impossibly far away.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: What helps me is to break the race into small pieces. I never think about forty-two kilometres. I think about reaching the next water station, or the next tree, or the next song in my headphones.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I also talk to myself, but kindly. If a friend was struggling, you'd say, you're doing well, keep going. So why do we speak so harshly to ourselves? Try being your own coach rather than your own critic.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Another thing: you should never compare yourself with the person next to you. Last year, a woman of seventy overtook me at kilometre thirty-five, and I was determined to catch her. I never did, and I ended the race exhausted. I learned that my race is my own.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: None of this is only about sport. Exams, interviews, difficult conversations, they all have a wall. If you know it's coming, and you have a plan, it becomes much less frightening.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: So, my advice is simple. Be patient, be kind to yourself, and take it one tree at a time. Thank you. Any questions?

parts.title: Part 4 · A podcast discussion
parts.intro: You will hear Minh and Helen discussing whether everyone should run a marathon.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Today's question is a big one: should everyone try to run a marathon at least once? Helen, I know you think so.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: I do, Minh, although I'd say it comes with conditions. I ran my first one at forty and it changed how I see myself. If I can do that, I thought, what else am I capable of?

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: See, I find that argument a bit romantic. A marathon is an enormous strain on the body. Doctors see a lot of knee and hip problems in people who push too hard.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: That's fair, and I'm not suggesting anyone just wakes up and runs forty-two kilometres. You need at least four or five months of training. But for most healthy people, it's perfectly safe if you build up slowly.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Even so, why a marathon? A ten-kilometre race gives you the same sense of achievement with a fraction of the commitment.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Because the commitment is the point. The race is one day, but the months of training change your habits, your sleep, your diet. That's the real benefit.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Hmm. I'd still argue that the cost matters too. Entry fees, shoes, travel, it all adds up. Not everyone can afford that.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Good point, I'll admit. Though running itself is almost free, and you could do a marathon distance on your own local roads. You don't need a fancy event.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Right, so we agree on one thing. The goal should be what suits each person, not what impresses other people.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Exactly. Do it for yourself, or don't do it at all.

questions.text: Why did Daniel start running?
options: He was bored with his job and needed a hobby
His doctor advised him to lose weight
He wanted to win races against his friends
A neighbour asked him to join a running club
questions.explanation: He says his doctor told him to lose weight. The neighbour only persuaded him to join a club later.

evidence.quote: my doctor told me to lose weight

questions.text: What mistake did Daniel make as a beginner?
options: Joining a running club far too early
Trying to go too far, too fast
Not eating enough pasta before each race
Running only in the evening after work
questions.explanation: He says most beginners try to go too far, too fast, and he got injured.

evidence.quote: trying to go too far, too fast

options: It taught him how to cook healthy meals before races

It lent him better shoes and a training plan
